text.p: Euro Disney profits jumped 77 percent in 1995/96, helped by record attendance at its attraction-packed Disneyland Paris theme park, but the debt-laden company said on Tuesday it was not out of the woods.

It said net income rose to 202 million francs ($39.69 million) in the year to September 30 from 114 million a year earlier, as a nine percent increase in revenues to five billion francs more than offset rising costs and finance charges on its 15.1 billion franc debt.
"We are proud of what has been accomplished in a difficult economic environment, particularly for the tourism industry," Euro Disney chairman Philippe Bourguignon said in a statement.
"Our public endorsement is definitely demonstrated."
But he said sluggish consumer spending, coupled with increases in financial costs, were clouding the outlook.
"Persistent weakness in the economy, constant pressure on our prices, and the strong increase in financial charges constitute several real challenges for the future, particularly in 1997," he said.
Euro Disney's stock, which rallied 7.5 percent on Monday ahead of the results, slid back 2.6 percent to 11.15 francs on the Paris bourse at 0920 GMT.
The company's results, marking Euro Disney's second consecutive year in the black, contain a double irony.

A nine percent rise in attendance to 11.7 million visitors last year and a slight increase in visitor spending confirm that the Disney park, which had been predicted to flop in Europe, is a winner. A third of the visitors had been to the park before.
Theme park revenues increased nine percent to 2.7 billion francs, and hotel revenues increased 11 percent to 2.0 billion francs as occupancy rates rose to 72 percent from 68 percent.
On the other hand, a 1994 financial restructuring hailed for having pulled the company from the brink of collapse now poses the biggest risk as its costs are gradually phased in.
Lease and financial charges rose 103 million francs to 568 million in 1995/96. The company has estimated they will rise by a further 200 million in 1996/97 and by 100 million in 1997/98.
From 1998/99, royalties and management fees to 39-percent owner The Walt Disney Co will also be reinstated.

But Bourguignon said in an interview with Reuters that the current year posed the greatest challenge, as the company had decided not to raise prices even though it would have to absorb the biggest one-time increase in financial charges.

He said the company was not holding any talks aimed at restructuring its debt. He also said the group maintained its policy of favouring the use of cashflow to reduce debt rather than pay a dividend for the next two or three years. "We think that would be more favourable to shareholders," he said.

Euro Disney, which lost more than seven billion francs in its first two years, emerged from the red for the first time last year after slashing its entry prices and adding new attractions like the Space Mountain rollercoaster.

But its recovery has been hampered by weak spending in Europe, and particularly in France, because of high unemployment and government austerity aimed at fulfilling the budget criteria for the creation in 1999 of a single European currency.

The economic environment has taken a heavy toll on leisure groups, most recently on the well-known French resort company Club Mediterranee, which predicted last month that its results for the peak summer season would be flat.

Euro Disney is struggling in this difficult context to maintain its momentum. It plans to mark its fifth anniversary this year with customary Disney fanfare, including the unveiling of a new castle in January and a springtime festival.

It is also proceeding with commercial and residential projects adjacent to the theme park that will be financed mostly by third parties. Euro Disney has previously said that, further down the line, it plans to build a second theme park.
($1=5.089 French Franc)
